Abstract Background  Maternal and newborn mortality remains a persistent global health issue, and most of these deaths are preventable through timely provision of Emergency Obstetric and Neonatal Care (EmONC). Despite the integration of EmONC into health systems, many low and middle-income countries struggle with suboptimal quality and readiness of services. This study aimed to assess the implementation of EmONC in community health centers (Puskesmas) in Jember, Indonesia, focusing on facility readiness and availability of the seven Basic EmONC (BEmONC) signal functions and the factors influencing service provision. Methods  A convergent mixed-methods study was conducted in 50 Puskesmas health facilities providing delivery services in Jember from January 1 to July 31, 2023. Quantitative data were collected using facility surveys adapted from the Rapid EmONC Assessment Tool. Qualitative data were gathered through semi-structured interviews with stakeholders (n = 12), patients (n = 10), and focus group discussions with midwives (n = 2). Descriptive statistics were used to summarize trends, and t-test or Mann-Whitney U test to compare between groups. Qualitative data were analyzed using inductive content analysis. Results  None of the Puskesmas met standards for fully functional BEmONC facilities. Among the seven BEmONC signal functions, parenteral uterotonics were most commonly provided (88% of facilities), while assisted vaginal delivery was not provided by any facility (0%). Surveyed facilities had a median of 70% (interquartile range 63–77%) of the 160 essential EmONC equipment and medications available. Key gaps were identified in essential medicines, equipment, provider training, and monitoring systems. Qualitative findings revealed barriers at systemic and facility levels, including insufficient provider training, inconsistent resource availability, and inadequate monitoring. Facilitators included growing community trust, existing infrastructure, and political commitment to maternal health.

​Background Reducing maternal and newborn mortality remains a critical global health challenge, despite being priori­ tized in both the Millennium Development Goals and the subsequent Sustainable Development Goal 3, Target 3.1, which aims to reduce the global maternal mortality ratio (MMR) to less than 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. Progress has been insufficient, with only 9 out of 95 high-mortality countries achieving the Millenium Devel­ opment Goals target of a two-thirds reduction in mater­ nal mortality by 2015 [1]. From 2000 to 2020, the global MMR declined by 34%, representing an average annual reduction of 2.1%, which is not sufficient to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals target by 2030. As of 2020, an estimated 287,000 women still died due to maternal causes annually, equivalent to 800 deaths every day [2].

Most maternal deaths result from complications during pregnancy or childbirth, with hemorrhage, sepsis, unsafe abortion, and obstructed labor accounting for over twothirds of global maternal mortality [3]. It is estimated that 15% of women will develop life-threatening compli­ cations during pregnancy and childbirth, many of which cannot be predicted or prevented [4, 5]. However, most complications can be successfully treated through the timely provision of quality emergency obstetric and neo­ natal care (EmONC) [6].

EmONC encompasses a set of lifesaving services that are essential for managing obstetric complications and preventing maternal and neonatal deaths [7]. The World Health Organization outlined two levels: Basic EmONC (BEmONC) and Comprehensive EmONC (CEmONC) [6]. BEmONC facilities provide seven “signal functions” which are key medical interventions used to treat direct obstetric complications that cause most maternal deaths. These signal functions include: administration of par­ enteral antibiotics, administration of parenteral anti­ convulsants, administration of parenteral uterotonics, manual removal of placenta, removal of retained prod­ ucts, assisted vaginal delivery (AVD), and basic neona­ tal resuscitation [6]. CEmONC facilities, in addition to providing BEmONC signal functions, should also be able to perform cesarean sections and provide blood trans­ fusions [6]. Evidence shows that quality EmONC can avert the majority of maternal deaths [8]. Basic EmONC alone can avert 40% of intrapartum-related newborn and maternal deaths [9].

Subsequently, many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) have integrated EmONC provision into their health services. Despite efforts to implement EmONC, significant challenges persist, with a widening gap in mortality rates between high-income and low-income settings. In 2020, the MMR in low-income countries was 430 per 100,000 live births, compared to just 12 per 100,000 in high-income countries. This gap is par­ ticularly concerning given that 95% of global maternal deaths occur in low and low-middle-income countries, where many countries lack the health system capacity to provide quality services [2]. Many LMICs struggle with inadequate facility readiness and suboptimal quality of services [10–17]. Therefore, the focus should be shifted from merely increasing access to improving the quality of maternal health services. Provision of quality health ser­ vices can save over eight million lives each year in LMICs [18].

Indonesia, a middle-income country, serves as an example of the challenges faced in providing quality EmONC services. Despite having high rates of skilled birth attendance (91%) and facility-based deliveries (74%), Indonesia faces a persistently high MMR of 186 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2020 [19, 20]. This para­ dox suggests that widespread access to midwifery ser­ vices has not translated into commensurate reductions in maternal mortality. Studies have shown that health ser­ vice access and characteristics account for 23% of the dif­ ference in MMR between high and low MMR provinces in Indonesia, with factors such as the density of doctors and distance to the nearest hospital playing significant roles [21].

The two leading causes of maternal deaths in Indonesia are hemorrhage and hypertensive disorder in pregnancy (pre-eclampsia and eclampsia), complications that are treatable with effective EmONC [22]. In response to these challenges, the Ministry of Health has integrated Basic EmONC into its primary healthcare system through a strategy known as PONED [23]. This approach designates certain community health centers in Indonesia, known as Puskesmas, as PONED and are required to provide 24/7 services and perform all seven BEmONC signal func­ tions [24]. For more complex cases, Puskesmas PONED can refer patients to Comprehensive EmONC facilities, known as PONEK hospitals. Addressing these challenges requires a comprehensive service delivery redesign approach, focusing on centralizing and strengthening EmONC services in strategically selected facilities. While these issues have been documented in both peer-reviewed and gray literature in the past, few recent studies examine how BEmONC operates in community health centers, especially in highmortality districts such as Jember, and integrate both quantitative and qualitative data to provide a comprehen­ sive view.

Therefore, we conducted a study assessing the imple­ mentation of BEmONC in Puskesmas health facilities in Jember, a regency district in East Java. In 2022, Jember recorded the highest number of maternal and neonatal deaths in the province. Given the complexity of EmONC implementation, we employed a mixed-methods approach to capture both measurable indicators and con­ textual factors. We used quantitative surveys to evaluate facility readiness and availability of the seven BEmONC signal functions, and qualitative interviews and focus group discussions to explore factors influencing ser­ vice provision. By integrating these complementary data sources, our research yields a more holistic understand­ ing on strengthening EmONC services in resource-lim­ ited settings and contributes to broader global efforts to reduce maternal mortality.

Methods Study setting This study was conducted in Jember, East Java, Indonesia, a district with a population of 2.6 million in 2023. Jem­ ber’s healthcare system includes 50 Puskesmas, of which 25 are designated as BEmONC facilities (Puskesmas PONED), and 6 hospitals designated as CEmONC facili­ ties (PONEK hospitals).

Study design We used a convergent mixed-methods approach, collect­ ing quantitative and qualitative data concurrently (Fig. 1). The quantitative component aimed to describe facility readiness and availability of BEmONC signal functions, while the qualitative component aimed to explore factors influencing service provision, focusing on barriers and facilitators. We first analyzed each dataset independently, then integrated the quantitative and qualitative findings using a joint display.

Data collection and sampling Quantitative We surveyed all 50 Puskesmas in Jember offering deliv­ ery services, representing the total population of com­ munity health centers in the district. Quantitative data were collected using a survey instrument adapted from the Rapid EmONC Assessment Tool developed by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the Averting Maternal Death and Disability program at Columbia University [31]. Data analysis Quantitative Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the avail­ ability of EmONC infrastructure, equipment, medi­ cations, and human resources, delivery trends, signal function provision, and complication management. For each facility, we calculated the percentage of items avail­ able overall and within each category defined by the Rapid EmONC Assessment Tool. We described availabil­ ity of services in Jember by presenting the median and interquartile ranges of these percentages across health facilities. As PONED facilities would be expected to be better equipped to handle obstetric emergencies and handle more obstetric and neonatal complications than regular Puskesmas (referred to as non-PONED facili­ ties), we assessed the difference between the two statis­ tically using t-tests for normally distributed continuous variables or Mann-Whitney U tests for non-normally distributed variables. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were conducted using Excel and R.

Indonesian context based on the Ministry of Health’s guidelines for EmONC implementation in Puskesmas [24] (see Additional file 1). The survey assessed facil­ ity readiness by measuring the availability of 160 key items (infrastructure, equipment, medications, human resources) and captured data on deliveries, obstetric and neonatal complications from January to July 2023. We recorded whether each facility provided each of the seven BEmONC signal functions at least once during the ref­ erence period (yes/no), with reasons for non-provision if applicable. The survey was completed by a designated representative from each Puskesmas, typically the head of the facility or the coordinator for maternal and child health services.

Qualitative We purposively sampled stakeholders, providers, and patients from eight Puskesmas PONED facilities. The facilities were identified in consultation with the Jem­ ber Department of Health, whose officials served as key informants. The facilities were chosen to capture varia­ tion in PONED program implementation across Jember, with consideration of delivery volume, level of active management of obstetric cases, and facility willingness to participate. This sampling strategy was designed to cap­ ture diverse perspectives and ensure representativeness.

We conducted 22 semi-structured interviews (12 stakeholders, 10 patients) and 2 focus group discussions (FGDs) with providers. Stakeholders included individu­ als who worked at the Jember Department of Health or held managerial roles in Puskesmas PONED for more than 1 year. Two stakeholder interviews were conducted at the Jember Department of Health with officials directly responsible for the PONED program (the Head of the Health Services Division and the Head of the Primary Care Sub-Division). Across the eight Puskesmas, stake­ holder interviews were conducted with 1–2 participants per facility, consisting of Heads of Puskesmas, PONED coordinators, and/or maternity ward coordinators.

Providers consisted of midwives who have more than 1 year of experience in Puskesmas PONED and were involved in EmONC provision. Each facility sent 1–2 providers to the FGDs, some of whom had also partici­ pated in the stakeholder interviews.

Patients were postpartum women who delivered within the past month, and experienced obstetric or neonatal complications, accessed PONED services, and attended antenatal or postnatal care at the Puskesmas. Patient interviews were conducted at the four higher-capacity facilities (1–4 patients per facility), where the volume of eligible cases permitted recruitment. Participants unwill­ ing to take part, employees not involved in PONED, or patients without documented obstetric/neonatal emer­ gencies were excluded.

Qualitative Qualitative data were analyzed using an inductive content analysis approach [32]. Four interview and FGD tran­ scripts were initially open-coded by the primary author to develop a preliminary codebook. This codebook was then refined and piloted to assess comprehensiveness and finalize the coding structure. The final codebook was applied to the entire dataset using Dedoose software (version 9.2, SocioCultural Research Consultants, LLC, Los Angeles, CA) by the primary author.

Two researchers (MCW and HG) independently reviewed the coded data using an inductive approach to identify patterns and construct a draft set of themes. Where the two researchers diverged in their interpreta­ tion, discrepancies were resolved through team discus­ sion until consensus was reached. The draft themes were then reviewed and discussed by the research team to confirm their labels, definitions, and illustrative quotes. Through an iterative process of discussion and refine­ ment, a final set of six themes was developed to capture the key findings from the qualitative data.

To enhance the trustworthiness of the qualitative findings, we employed several established strategies. Credibility was supported through triangulation of per­ spectives across our three participant groups (stake­ holders, providers, and patients) and through member checking of preliminary findings with a subset of stake­ holder participants. Dependability and confirmability were supported through peer debriefing and weekly team review meetings throughout coding and analysis. Data saturation was determined when no new themes emerged from the analysis of additional transcripts.

We examined the extent to which qualitative themes either corroborated or provided additional context for the gaps in service provision and readiness identified by our quantitative survey, and conversely, we explored instances where the quantitative findings helped to explain the challenges described in the qualitative data. We subsequently synthesized these results in a joint

Gaps in facility readiness Providers and stakeholders described several connected gaps in the readiness of Puskesmas to deliver EmONC services. Healthcare providers expressed an urgent desire for updated EmONC training, pointing to insuf­ ficient provider training as a key concern. Although the quantitative results did not identify “lack of training” as a direct barrier, interviews revealed a clear need for refresher courses and mentoring, particularly for low-fre­ quency, high-risk procedures. Staff turnover has exacer­ bated the issue, with trained personnel leaving and their replacements lacking the necessary training, and this gap directly impacts providers’ confidence and service capa­ bility to the extent that some are willing to self-fund their training.

We face human resource challenges. We need PONED training, but no one is trained. Ideally, the training should be provided from higher authorities. We’re unsure of the exact challenges. Closely tied to these training gaps is inconsistent resource availability at the facility level. Health facilities experience inconsistent availability of equipment which undermines the provision of effective EmONC services, and the challenge is exacerbated by inadequate main­ tenance services for broken equipment. There are also instances where the available equipment is not used, pri­ marily due to a lack of personnel trained to operate it.

Growing trust in puskesmas services Patients described how community perceptions of Pusk­ esmas have shifted over time, with overcoming distrust through patient-provider relationships emerging as a key dynamic. Previously, patients tended to distrust care at government-funded Puskesmas, associating free services with poor quality. Strong patient-provider rela­ tionships have been crucial in overcoming this skepti­ cism and facilitating PONED implementation. Trust often develops during antenatal care, where consistent, quality interactions with midwives help patients over­ come apprehensions about birthing at Puskesmas. Con­ sequently, these relationships establish Puskesmas as a trusted source for maternal services, enhancing adher­ ence to medical advice.

These relationships also have a broader community effect, with positive experiences driving demand: improved services at Puskesmas have positively shifted community perceptions, making nearby community health centers more attractive for childbirth to patients compared to distant hospitals. As more patients have positive experiences delivering at Puskesmas, they share their stories with others in the community, and this rip­ ple effect has led to an increased demand for giving birth at these facilities.

Discussion This study revealed critical gaps in BEmONC readiness, as well as systemic barriers to service delivery in Jember. None of the designated BEmONC facilities in Jember met the UNFPA standard for fully functional EmONC

facilities [31]. This was primarily due to the non-provi­ sion of AVD because of local restrictions, although pro­ vision of other functions was also lacking. This finding is consistent with evaluations from other LMICs, which have documented discrepancies between the number of designated EmONC facilities and their actual func­ tionality [10–17]. Interpreted through the WHO Health Systems Building Blocks framework [33], the barriers we identified in Jember span five of the six building blocks: financing (decentralization of financial management), workforce (insufficient provider training), medical prod­ ucts and equipment (inconsistent resource availability), information systems (inadequate monitoring and evalu­ ation), and governance and service delivery (complex conditions affecting providers’ decision-making). This pattern indicates that the gaps in EmONC provision cut across interrelated parts of the health system. At the same time, community trust, political will, and exist­ ing physical and digital infrastructure support EmONC implementation.

As in Jember, AVD is often the least provided signal function in other low and middle-income settings [12– 14, 17, 34]. This reflects a global trend of declining use of AVD especially in LMICs, largely due to the method’s

Among these, certain medication such as parenteral antibiotics showed very low availability, with procaine penicillin injections at 1 (2%) facility, ampicillin injections at 5 (10%), gentamicin injections at 6 (13%), and metronidazole injections at 15 (31%). Only 9 (19%) facilities reported having Manual Vacuum Aspirator kits and vacuum extractors. Four (16%) facilities cited lack of equipment as a reason for not performing an EmONC signal function.

However, it is crucial to understand that AVD, when performed correctly, can be a lifesaving intervention in cases of complications during the second stage of labor or in emergencies where access to emergency caesarean section is lacking [36]. Previous researchers have identi­ fied several potential drivers for the underuse of AVD in LMICs, including lack of functioning equipment, insuffi­ cient staff training in selecting appropriate candidates for AVD or performing the procedure, suboptimal supervi­ sion and support, and fear of litigation in case of adverse outcomes [36]. These patterns align closely with the broader theme of our qualitative findings in Jember. The non-existence of AVD in Jember represents a significant missed opportunity in EmONC provision, pointing to a need for targeted training and awareness programs for health providers, potentially leading to a reintroduction of AVD.

Although none of the surveyed facilities reported lack of training as a reason for not providing a specific signal function (Table 3), our qualitative data revealed a more nuanced picture: providers feel inadequately prepared to manage emergencies without ongoing professional devel­ opment. In other words, while they may technically know how to perform the procedures, they do not feel confi­ dent or comfortable managing these emergencies without regular refresher training. This situation is further exac­ erbated by the low monthly delivery volumes observed even in Puskesmas designated as BEmONC, which pro­ vide fewer opportunity to practice and reinforce these skills, thereby contributing to a risk-averse culture in handling obstetrics emergency. Studies have shown that low delivery volume is consistently associated with poor quality of care in basic maternal health services, includ­ ing some BEmONC signal functions [37], while providers working in higher-level facilities with greater exposure to complicated cases demonstrate higher EmONC knowl­ edge scores compared to those in lower-level facili­ ties [38]. Additionally, limited opportunities to manage obstetric emergencies may lead to a gradual erosion of skills [39], whereas frequent performance of these proce­ dures is linked to higher levels of confidence [40].

The situation in Jember highlights the inadequacy of Indonesia’s current EmONC implementation model, par­ ticularly the PONED program’s approach of designating facilities as BEmONC without ensuring their functional­ ity. To address these challenges, we propose adopting a service delivery redesign (SDR) approach, as suggested by the 2018 Lancet Global Health Commission on High- Quality Health Systems [18]. This approach involves concentrating both obstetric and neonatal services and improvement efforts in fewer facilities to improve health system efficiency [41]. Our recommendation are thus: first, conduct a nationwide mapping exercise to

identify and prioritize “highly functional” BEmONC facilities (Puskesmas PONED). These would be facilities with higher delivery volumes, strategic locations, or those receiving a higher number of referrals. These prioritized facilities should then receive targeted resource alloca­ tion and quality improvement initiatives. Simultaneously, existing non-functional Puskesmas PONED should undergo a thorough re-evaluation to determine whether these facilities should be downgraded to regular Pusk­ esmas status or receive targeted interventions to meet BEmONC standards, taking into account the constraints of limited resources. Second, enhance providers’ capacity through targeted training, particularly in BEmONC facil­ ities, to manage certain complications and reduce refer­ rals to higher-level facilities. This could involve in-service training methods such as low-dose, high-frequency ses­ sions to maintain competence in managing less common obstetric emergencies [42], and potentially reintroducing AVD for providers [35]. Third, creating demand by col­ laborating with private practice midwives, who assist a significant proportion of deliveries in Indonesia [43], to encourage patients to deliver in these facilities [44]. This would improve delivery volumes in BEmONC facili­ ties and enhance provider skills through increased case exposure.

Although various models of SDR have been discussed for over a decade in Indonesia, widespread adoption remains limited. Several models have been implemented in other low income settings [45, 46]. One such model in Tanzania of decentralizing CEmONC by upgrad­ ing primary care facilities showed promise in improv­ ing maternal health outcomes [47]. Implementing such a redesign will require substantial government commit­ ment, adequate resource allocation, and active commu­ nity engagement to ensure its success and sustainability, while avoiding the pitfall of creating yet another wellintentioned but ineffective policy that fails to address root issues.

Our study’s primary contribution lies in examining BEmONC services in Jember, a high-mortality district that has received limited attention in previous research, combining both quantitative and qualitative data to cap­ ture system-wide and on-the-ground realities. In doing so, we offer current insights that build on past research while pinpointing actionable strategies such as SDR and targeted provider training that can strengthen BEmONC services in similar contexts. Nonetheless, our reliance on self-reported data and the cross-sectional design limits the ability to draw causal inferences or observe trends over time. Future research should adopt longitudinal approaches to evaluate the impact and sustainability of policy interventions on EmONC provision and maternal health outcomes in Indonesia. Additionally, implementa­ tion research on targeted training programs and resource

Conclusion In conclusion, this study reveals significant challenges in the implementation of EmONC services in Jember, Indonesia, reflecting broader issues within the coun­ try’s maternal health system. The absence of fully func­ tional BEmONC facilities, compounded by low delivery volumes and insufficient provider training, undermines efforts to reduce maternal mortality. To address these challenges, we propose a comprehensive service delivery redesign approach, focusing on centralizing and strength­ ening EmONC services in strategically selected facilities. This approach, while requiring substantial commitment and paradigm shift in healthcare delivery, has the poten­ tial to significantly improve the quality and accessibility of maternal care within resource constraints. The success of this approach could serve as a model for other regions facing similar challenges in EmONC provision.

# Devastating pregnancy outcomes in the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic

**Authors:** Manggala P. Wardhana; Maria C. Wijaya; Salsabila N. Rifdah; Ifan A. Wafa; Dahlia Ningrum; Erry G. Dachlan

**Affiliations:** 1 Doctoral Program of Medical Science, Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Airlangga, Indonesia | 2 Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Airlangga – Dr. Soetomo Academic General Hospital, Indonesia | 3 Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Airlangga – Dr. Soetomo Academic General Hospital, Indonesia | 4 Resident in Training, Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Airlangga, Indonesia

## Abstract

This study analyzed pregnancy outcomes in postpartum women who were infected with COVID-19 during their pregnancy in resource-limited settings during the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic.

This cross-sectional study included all pregnant women with COVID-19 at a tertiary referral hospital in Surabaya, Indonesia, from June to August 2021. Patients were classified according to clinical presentation into asymptomatic-mild, moderate, and severe-critical. Data regarding their basic maternal characteristics, clinical symptoms, delivery, and neonatal outcomes were collected and analyzed across these severity levels through ANOVA, Kruskal–Wallis, or Mann–Whitney U test by incorporating SPSS Statistics software version 29.0.

During the second wave of COVID-19 in Indonesia, a total of 184 COVID-19 cases were reported, with high mortality rate (22%). Only 26.6% of these cases were asymptomatic-mild, and the remaining 73.4% had more severe conditions. The severe-critical group had significantly lower gestational age, slower onset of diseases/symptoms, and higher maternal death proportions than the other two groups (P < 0.001). Clinical symptoms, vital signs, and inflammatory markers (NLR, CRP, and procalcitonin) were also significantly worse in the severe-critical group than in the other groups (P < 0.05). Consequently, severe cases showed a higher cesarean section rate (P = 0.034), lower birth weight, lower Apgar score, higher incidence of perinatal deaths (P < 0.001), and higher incidence of neonatal support (P = 0.003).

The study's findings specified the devastating consequences of second wave of COVID-19 in a resource-limited setting. Focus on improving the health system and health facilities’ capacity is warranted to anticipate all possibilities of other pandemics in the future.

## Introduction

Since the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 (or SARS-CoV-2) a pandemic in March 2020, many new variants of this disease have emerged. Variant B.1.617.2, more popularly known as the Delta variant, caught global attention due to its high transmissibility, severe clinical outcomes, and breakthrough infections among the vaccinated population.[1] First identified in India at the end of 2020, the COVID-19 Delta variant was believed to be one of Indonesia's leading contributors to the second wave of infection.[2] In June 2021, the number of daily new confirmed cases increased exponentially in Indonesia.[3] By August 2, 2021, Indonesia had the most COVID-19 infections and many related deaths—with 6.47 confirmed new deaths per million people daily, the country ranked ninth in the world.[3] This condition also impacted vulnerable pregnant women who require specific management as health facilities struggled due to the abrupt increase in new cases with high mortality during the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic.

COVID-19 infection in pregnancy has been associated with more adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes compared to normal pregnant women.[4] Extensive data from CDC also indicate that pregnant women have an increased risk of severe COVID-19-associated illness compared to non-pregnant women.[5] This may be due to physiological changes that arise during pregnancy, which increase pregnant women's risk of suffering severe COVID-19 infections.[6] Nevertheless, most patients who arrived at hospitals were asymptomatic and adequately managed.[7] The nine-month report of the initial COVID-19 attack in one of Indonesia's tertiary hospitals also showed a similar condition, with only 10.1% severe COVID-19 conditions reported in obstetric cases during admission.[8] However, second-wave conditions that are believed to be dominated by Delta variant mutations increased the degree of maternal severity and death in India.[9]

There is currently finite epidemiological study available that provides evidence of the situation amid the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic in obstetric services in Indonesia. Therefore, this study aims to describe pregnancy outcomes among pregnant women with COVID-19 in one tertiary care hospital in Indonesia, which may represent the extent of the disturbances that occur in limited-resource settings country.

## Materials and Methods

### Study design and setting

This cross-sectional study was conducted at Dr. Soetomo General Academic Hospital, Surabaya, Indonesia, during the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic (June to August 2021).

### Study participants and sampling

This study included 184 postpartum women who were infected with COVID-19 during their pregnancy. COVID-19 was diagnosed using a real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using the Abbott m2000 with an Abbott RealTime SARS-CoV-2 assay. All pregnant patients presented to triage were tested for COVID-19 infection using a nasopharyngeal swab, with either a PCR test or antigen swab.

### Data collection tool and technique

Basic maternal characteristics data, including parity, maternal age, gestational age, maternal deaths, length of stay, and referral status, were collected from electronic medical records. Referral status was classified into self-admission, referred, or forced referral. A forced referral is a referral for patients who previously went to a hospital but were rejected due to overloaded capacity and, therefore, were told to look for other hospitals by themselves without inter-hospital communication. Obstetrical outcome data included conservative treatment, abortus, labor and delivery, and postpartum treatment. Data on patient comorbidities, such as hypertension in pregnancy, obesity, and diabetes, were also obtained. Data regarding COVID-19 disease presentation, including clinical symptoms, laboratory results, radiographic findings, oxygen support, and intensive care admission status were also collected. COVID-19 disease severity was classified according to World Health Organization criteria.[10] However, this study divides severity into asymptomatic-mild, moderate, and severe-critical. The severity level was assessed upon admission rather than when the condition was at its worst. The oxygen support level was reported twice: upon admission and at the highest level. The onset of disease was calculated from the onset of symptoms until hospital admission or (if asymptomatic) from the positive PCR test result date.

Delivery and neonatal outcomes were obtained in patients who delivered children. Neonatal outcomes included perinatal death, positive neonatal COVID-19 infection, and neonatal support. Apgar score and birth weight were also obtained as outcome indicators in live birth cases. Perinatal death is defined as the death of a baby between 22 weeks of gestation (or weighing 500 g) and seven days after birth.[11] Neonatal COVID-19 infection is defined as a positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR test result from an oral swab specimen taken from neonates.

Data were analyzed using SPSS version 29 (serial number: #D0EWPLL-272-128-1). Descriptive statistics in categorical variables were presented using numbers (percentages), whereas mean (±SD) and median (min-max) were used for numerical variables. Multivariable modeling was used to evaluate associations between severity levels and outcomes. Parametric variables were tested using ANOVA. The Kruskal–Wallis test was used for nonparametric variables, followed by the Mann–Whitney U test if a significant association was found. A P-value of <0.05 was considered significant.

### Ethical consideration

This study has been approved by the ethical committee of Dr. Soetomo General Academic Hospital Surabaya (No. 0896/LOE/301.4.2/IV/2022). Informed consent was obtained from all patients before the study began.

## Results

The first case of pregnant patients with COVID-19 in the hospital was reported in April 2020. The number of cases continued to rise, peaking in June 2020. Afterward, the number of cases decreased and remained relatively stable until May 2021. Figure 1 shows that the second wave of COVID-19 began in May 2021, culminated in July 2021, and continued through August 2021.

*Figure 1: Maternal COVID-19 cases in Dr. Soetomo General Hospital, Surabaya, between April 2020 and August 2021*

A total of 184 pregnant women tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 infection during the second wave (from June to August 2021) and presented a very high mortality rate (42 maternal deaths or 22%). Of these, moderate severity was the most common severity level (98 cases, 53.2%), whereas 49 cases (26.6%) were classified as asymptomatic-mild and 37 (20.1%) as severe-critical. We analyzed all the maternal and neonatal data based on these three severity-level groups. The case distribution is shown in Figure 2.

## Discussion

This cohort comprised pregnant patients at Dr. Soetomo General Academic Hospital who tested positive for COVID-19 between June and August 2021. During this period, many COVID-19 cases worldwide were attributed to the Delta variant.[12912] This variant was first identified in Indonesia in May 2021 and immediately became the dominant variant responsible for the rising number of COVID-19 cases.[12] On June 13, the Ministry of Health reported that the Delta variant had been circulating in six provinces in Indonesia, namely DKI Jakarta, East Java, Central Java, South Sumatra, Central Kalimantan, and East Kalimantan. Between June and August 2021, the number of COVID-19 daily new confirmed cases continued to rise exponentially, eventually surpassing the highest number of daily cases previously recorded in the country. The previous highest number of daily new confirmed cases was 14,518 on January 30, 2021. On July 15, 2021, the number of new daily cases was 56,757, representing a four-fold increase.[13]

One of the contributing factors to the second wave was the Eid-al-Fitr holidays, during which people return to their hometown (mudik). This massive exodus occurred in mid-May despite government restrictions intended to prevent it. By this time, 41 million COVID-19 vaccine doses had been administered to the Indonesian population. However, pregnant women were not yet included in the target population for COVID-19 vaccination. On August 2, 2021, the Ministry of Health finally approved vaccinations for pregnant women; however, this decision may have been made too late.

Compared to a previous report of SARS-CoV-2 infections in pregnant women during the first wave in Indonesia, during which most cases were asymptomatic-mild,[8] most cases during the second wave were of moderate to critical severity (73.37%). Several studies also found a significant increase in the proportion of severe or critical illness in pregnant women with COVID-19 during the Delta wave.[9141516] Furthermore, most patients came to the hospital either by themselves or by forced referral (61.4%) without being accompanied by any health worker. These patients came to our tertiary-level hospital after being rejected for primary or secondary-level care due to overloaded capacities in other hospitals. This signaled the collapse of health facilities at the secondary level, especially those developed specifically to provide obstetric services. Sudden increases in the number and severity of cases may have immensely contributed to this disaster.

Unlike during the first wave, most patients in this study were symptomatic (77.2%), and significantly worse vital signs were accompanied by deteriorating O2 peripheral saturation in severe-critical cases. A significant increase in supplementary oxygen support was also observed in more severe cases. However, this number does not reflect the reality of the situation, which may be even worse. Many patients who were presented to the hospital with severe-critical symptoms and oxygen desaturation (40.5%) were unable to receive the oxygen support they needed since the hospital's resources were depleted. Many patients quickly worsened, resulting in intensive care admission in more than a quarter of all patients (26.1%).

The need for additional oxygen support was detected during treatment compared to admission; the need for ventilators during treatment was eight times higher than during admission. Compared to the previous variant, infections from the Delta variant have a higher infectiousness capacity with a high ability of virus replication of up to 1000 times.[17] These factors resulted in a severe clinical situation during the second wave, which was dominated by the Delta variant.[1418]

The maternal death rate in this study (22%) was quite high. Chaudhary et al.[19] found that the maternal death rate during the second wave of COVID-19 was significantly higher compared to the first wave. Mahajan et al.[9] also reported a higher maternal mortality ratio during the second wave. Similarly, the morality rate reported in this study is more than three times higher than that reported in our previous study, which was conducted during the first wave.[8] Of 42 patients, six died during conservative management. Of these six deaths, four were caused by pre-viable fetuses, and one was due to intrauterine fetal death. The other death was a case of a quick progression of disease severity that caused the patient to die shortly after arriving at the hospital before termination could be performed.

The onset of symptoms was significantly longer in severe-critical conditions than in other conditions, with a median of seven days. This result is consistent with several previous studies showing that upper respiratory symptoms at the beginning of COVID-19 appear in the first five to six days.[20] Although most patients experience only mild symptoms, some develop pneumonia with dyspnea on the eighth day (IQR 5–13 days) and experience ARDS conditions on the ninth day.[21] The Delta variant may produce a faster onset, given the higher replication rate of this variant and the shortened period between exposure and positive PCR test compared to previously reported variants.[17] Other conditions, such as the patient's fear that there may be no hospital beds, made patients delay seeking care and caring for themselves (inadequately) at home. Because these patients did not go to the hospital promptly after experiencing symptoms, most patients were admitted while already in a severe condition.

Previous studies have stated that NLR, CRP, and procalcitonin are sensitive markers for the progression toward critical conditions in pregnant patients with COVID-19.[2223] Our findings agree with previous studies highlighting that NLR, CRP, and procalcitonin lab results differed significantly for different severity levels. Leukocytosis, lymphocytes, and D-Dimer parameters, which have often been used as markers of COVID-19 severity in other studies,[24] were not found in this study. The physiology of pregnancy also greatly alters the normal values of these parameters; therefore, additional care must be taken when considering these parameters as COVID-19 severity indicators. Some hematological changes due to physiological stress from pregnancy[25] and hypercoagulability conditions[26] can make it difficult to use this parameter as a severity indicator.

We also found that the median gestation age in severe-critical patients was significantly lower than in other patients at 31 weeks. This result is consistent with a study by UTMB, which found that pregnant COVID-19 patients during the Delta wave were more likely to be symptomatic and have a lower gestational age at the time of diagnosis than during the first wave.[27] Singh et al.[28] also found a significantly lower gestation period upon admission during the second wave compared to the first wave. As the maternal condition worsened, so did the condition of the neonate, as indicated by a significantly lower birthweight, lower neonatal Apgar score, and higher incidence of perinatal death.

This condition is also exacerbated by the maternal hypoxia that occurs in severe conditions. According to the previous studies, COVID-19 can increase the severe perinatal and mortality index by up to 2.14 times.[4] The vertical transmission of COVID-19 was obtained in 5.8% of cases in this study and was not influenced by COVID-19 severity. This condition is less prominent than indicated by multinational research by Giuliani, who showed perinatal transmission of up to 9.5%.[29] Conversely, the findings of current study are higher than the findings of other studies.[30] Generally, the perinatal transmission of COVID-19 is still poorly understood. Furthermore, different conditions can occur, including the possibility of in-utero exposure interval, which is correlated with a 4.5 times higher risk of neonatal COVID-19.[29]

To our knowledge, this is the first study characterizing the condition of the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic in obstetric services at a large center in Indonesia. Therefore, this study may accurately represent the magnitude of the disturbances that occur in a country with limited resources. Although the location of this study was the main referral hospital for COVID-19 cases in the second-largest province in Indonesia, a limitation of this study is that it was conducted in a single center. Hence, it is difficult to generalize the findings to other institutions.

Further, this study did not apply universal screening for all admitted obstetric patients, which would have detected asymptomatic COVID-19 cases. However, the hospital had implemented a strict screening procedure by which patient history and symptoms were evaluated and antigen swabs and chest X-rays were performed on all patients. The results of these procedures were used to determine if a PCR swab examination was necessary. According to the previous study, this screening procedure accurately identifies cases.[8]

This research highlights the devastating consequences of COVID-19 second wave pandemic in Indonesia due to the surging number of cases combined with the insufficiency of health facilities. The unexpected load on the health system caused many health facilities to collapse. The maternal deaths that occurred during this period could have been prevented if the weaknesses in the health care system had been addressed and preparations had been made. Although reports from several developed countries with more controlled pandemic conditions found no differences in maternal deaths,[3132] some specific studies, such as one conducted in Bahia, Brazil, showed an increase in maternal mortality due to the COVID-19 pandemic.[33] This research is expected to provide an important lesson to all stakeholders, especially in countries with limited resources, to help them strengthen the health system and increase the capacity of health facilities so that this tragedy does not reoccur.

## Conclusions

In conclusion, there were devastating maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality during the second wave of COVID-19 in Indonesia, which was dominated by the Delta variant. Contrary to reports during the first wave, most cases during the second wave were moderate to severe. There was also a higher maternal death rate; worse symptoms, vital signs, inflammatory markers (NLR, CRP, and procalcitonin), and pneumonia; a higher need for oxygen support; and intensive care for patients with severe conditions. Lower gestational age, birth weight, and Apgar scores with a higher incidence of neonatal death occurred in severe-critical conditions. More focus needs to be given to preparing obstetric health capacity and controlling the pandemic curve to anticipate all possibilities of other pandemics in the future.
